In software and enterprise data platform development, Product Managers (PMs), Product Owners (POs), and Business Analysts (BAs) produce a **layered chain of deliverables** [1]. This chain establishes a clear progression from high-level business justification to detailed functional behavior and technical data constraints [1, 2]. 

While generic software projects rely primarily on traditional system specifications, **enterprise data platforms require a distinct family of data-specific and governance artifacts** to prevent the platform from degenerating into a chaotic "data swamp" [1, 3].

The standard output documents, specifications, and deliverables are categorized below by the role primarily responsible for authoring and maintaining them:

---

### 1. Product Manager (PM) Deliverables
The Product Manager focuses on the strategic "why" and the overall "what" of the product from a market and user value perspective [3, 4].

*   **Business Case / Business Justification Document:** 
    *   *What it is:* A dynamic economic feasibility study that justifies why the organization should invest in the initiative [3].
    *   *What it contains:* Strategic alignment, options considered (including "doing nothing"), expected financial/non-financial benefits, cost estimates, and risk analyses [3].
    *   *Sequence:* This is the first document produced and must be approved before any detailed requirements work begins [3].
*   **Product Requirements Document (PRD):** 
    *   *What it is:* A high-level blueprint of the product's overall purpose, target audience, and features [4].
    *   *What it contains:* Problem statements, user personas, success metrics (quantitative KPIs), high-level feature descriptions, and out-of-scope items [4].
*   **Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM) / Scope Oversight:** 
    *   *What it is:* A mapping table that links every requirement back to its business origin and forward to its implementation and test cases [5]. While the BA physically maintains the RTM, the PM uses it for high-level scope and impact management [5].

---

### 2. Product Owner (PO) Deliverables
The Product Owner operates predominantly in agile environments, translating the PM's high-level PRD features into buildable, technical developer increments [6, 7].

*   **User Stories & Acceptance Criteria:** 
    *   *What it is:* Short, user-centric feature descriptions following the standard *"As a... I want... so that..."* format, paired with explicit, testable "Definition of Done" criteria [6].
    *   *Data Platform Specifics:* For data pipelines or backend data work, the PO adapts these stories to include **data-specific acceptance criteria**, such as row-count reconciliation, expected null-handling behavior, and transformation correctness [6].
*   **Product Backlog:** 
    *   *What it is:* A prioritized backlog of user stories and technical tasks, organized to decompose features into iterative sprints [6, 7].

---

### 3. Business Analyst (BA) Deliverables
The Business Analyst is the "Voice of the Business," capturing detailed operational processes, logical system requirements, and translating them for the technical engineering team [4, 8].

*   **Business Requirements Document (BRD):** 
    *   *What it is:* A plain-language record of *what* the business needs and *why*, explicitly keeping technical design details out of scope [8].
    *   *What it contains:* Project objectives, "As-Is" vs. "To-Be" process workflows, prioritized business needs, and cost-benefit appraisals [8].
*   **Functional Requirements Specification (FRS) / System Requirements Specification (SRS):** 
    *   *What it is:* A granular, unambiguous description of *how* the system must behave to satisfy the BRD, often utilizing uniquely identified "shall" statements [4].
*   **Non-Functional Requirements (NFR) Documentation:** 
    *   *What it is:* Documentation of the solution's quality attributes [9].
    *   *Data Platform Specifics:* For data platform architectures, the BA documents critical data volume and ingestion throughput limits, query/retrieval latency SLAs, retention/archival windows, and field-level security constraints (such as data masking and encryption rules) [9].

---

### 4. Specialized Data Platform & Governance Deliverables
When scoping an enterprise data platform, BAs and PMs must collaborate with Data Architects, Governance Leads, and Data Stewards to produce a highly specialized family of data-specific deliverables [1, 10]:

*   **Data Dictionary (BA-Owned):** Standardizes the definition, unique name, aliases, values, and composite structural rules for every technical data element across target data sources [1, 11].
*   **Source-to-Target Mapping (STM) (Joint BA & Architect-Owned):** A detailed, field-level blueprint defining exactly how fields in upstream source systems correspond to fields in the target data warehouse or lakehouse, capturing explicit logical transformation rules, nullability, default values, and format conversions [1, 12].
*   **Data Quality Requirements (Joint BA & Data Steward-Owned):** Documented, measurable expectations for the fitness-for-use of data, defined against DAMA-DMBOK's canonical six dimensions: accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, uniqueness, and validity [13].
*   **Business Glossary (Data Steward-Owned):** The governed, enterprise-wide system of record for standard business terms [14]. *This is kept strictly distinct from the technical Data Dictionary* to ensure business terminology (like what defines an "active customer") is standardized across different business units, preventing trust-destroying reporting discrepancies [10, 14].
